editorNote: Coleco is betting that a computer, tape drive, word processor and printer can arrive as one family-room package. Meanwhile, arcades turn to animation and Electronic Arts gives designers star billing.
morningLine: This week in 1983: Adam becomes the summer’s most talked-about computer, Dragon’s Lair draws crowds, and Electronic Arts’ first games reach reviewers.

lead.headline: Coleco’s Adam Promises a Complete Computer for Under $600
lead.dek: The summer CES sensation combines game compatibility, high-capacity tape, word processing and a daisy-wheel printer in one mass-market package.
body: The most talked-about personal computer of the summer is not merely a keyboard in a box. Coleco’s Adam, the lead item in the July 3 Arcade Express after its Consumer Electronics Show debut, is being pitched as a complete household system: computer, keyboard, high-capacity tape storage, word processing, joysticks and a daisy-wheel printer for a promised price below $600.

Inside, the Z80-family machine carries 80K of memory expandable to 144K, with 16K reserved for video. Its graphics system offers a 256-by-192 display and 32 sprites, while ColecoVision cartridge compatibility gives the newcomer a ready-made game shelf. Coleco also promises an expansion path below $450 for owners of its existing console.

The unusual piece is Coleco’s Digital Data Pack. Each proprietary cassette is rated for 500K, with transfer speeds claimed at eight to sixteen times those of conventional computer cassette systems. One drive is built into the package and a second was planned as an option. SmartWriter word processing lives in the system, making the bundled printer part of Adam’s identity rather than an accessory saved for later.

That integration is also the gamble. Popular Science cautioned that the demonstrated machines were prototypes, not tested production units, and Creative Computing singled out the proprietary tape format as Adam’s largest risk. A family buying into the package would depend on Coleco’s drives and media as well as its computer.

Even with those questions, Adam changes the sales-floor argument. Commodore can sell a bare 64 for far less, while Atari is bundling a writing system of its own. Coleco’s wager is that shoppers will pay for a computer that looks useful the moment the carton opens—and still plays the cartridges they already know.

stories.headline: The $600 System Becomes the New Battleground
stories.dek: Atari bundles writing tools while Commodore’s falling street price forces every home-computer maker to explain the whole package.
body: Adam arrives in a market where memory totals alone no longer settle the sale. Atari’s $600 Writing System combines a 600XL, AtariWriter, a guide, paper and a 20-character-per-second letter-quality printer, though buyers must still add storage and a television. Commodore 64 street prices, meanwhile, have been reported as low as $200.

That spread captures the market’s two strategies: sell the least expensive capable computer, or wrap the computer in enough useful equipment to justify a larger ticket. Mattel’s Aquarius and television offer joined the bundle race, while retailers marked down older Atari hardware with startling aggression. The result is a shelf crowded with packages whose similar prices conceal very different definitions of “complete.”

stories.headline: Dragon’s Lair Turns the Arcade into a Cartoon Theater
stories.dek: Don Bluth animation and LaserDisc branching give players pictures ordinary coin-op hardware cannot draw.
body: Cinematronics’ Dragon’s Lair, released to American arcades June 19, remains the most conspicuous new cabinet of early July. Developed by Advanced Microcomputer Systems with animation from Don Bluth’s studio, it trades real-time sprite drawing for hand-animated scenes stored on LaserDisc.

Players guide Dirk the Daring with timed joystick and sword-button choices, sending the disc to the next success—or comic death—sequence. The limited choices are hidden by lavish motion and color. In a year of game-industry contraction, the cabinet is a premium bet that spectacle can bring crowds back to the arcade.

stories.headline: Electronic Arts Gives Designers Star Billing
stories.dek: M.U.L.E. and a striking first wave of games treat programmers like recording artists.
body: The July–August Computer Gaming World finds Electronic Arts’ first wave in reviewers’ hands. Dan Bunten’s M.U.L.E. turns settlement economics into competitive multiplayer play as prospectors develop land, outfit robotic workers and bargain over resources at auction.

Alongside it, titles including Archon, Axis Assassin, Hard Hat Mack, Pinball Construction Set and Worms? arrive in oversized, album-like packages that foreground their creators. Exact retail months vary in later catalogs, but the period magazine makes the larger shift plain: a new publisher is selling computer games as authored works, not anonymous cartridges.

worldAnchor.headline: Maine schoolgirl arrives in Moscow on a mission for peace
worldAnchor.summary: Eleven-year-old Samantha Smith arrived in Moscow July 8 after Soviet leader Yuri Andropov invited her to tour the USSR in response to her letter asking why the two countries might go to war.
